paragraphs.text: Intermediate junctional epidermolysis bullosa-5A (JEB5A) is an autosomal recessive mucocutaneous blistering disorder caused by defects in integrin beta-4, a component of the alpha-6/beta-4 integrin of the hemidesmosome. Unlike the usually fatal form of epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia, affected individuals survive beyond infancy and have relatively mild skin involvement. Pyloric atresia may be present (Mellerio et al., 1998) or absent (Inoue et al., 2000; Jonkman et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Jonkman et al. (2002) reported a 49-year-old woman who had had mild blistering of the hands and feet from birth, nail dystrophy with onychogryposis, and enamel hypoplasia. She did not have alopecia and had no history of pyloric atresia. The clinical picture was predominantly that of epidermolysis bullosa simplex. Electron microscopy and antigen mapping of a skin blister showed intraepidermal separation low in the basal keratinocytes, through the attachment plaque of the hemidesmosome. Immunofluorescence microscopy showed absent binding of monoclonal antibody 450-11A, which recognizes the third fibronectin type III repeat in the intracellular domain of integrin beta-4, and reduced binding of antibodies recognizing epitopes at the amino- and carboxy-terminal ends of the protein.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated patients with mild EB-PA who survived into early childhood, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene. One patient carried a splice site mutation in exon 30 (3793+1G-A) and a nonsense mutation in exon 36 (W1478X). The other carried a missense mutation in exon 3 (C38R) and a 1-bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG). The nonsense and deletion mutations were predicted to markedly reduce beta-4 integrin mRNA levels. The authors suggested that the missense or splice site mutation on the second allele might allow synthesis of some functional, though perturbed, beta-4 polypeptide.

paragraphs.text: In a 49-year-old woman with a mild phenotype that mainly resembled epidermolysis bullosa simplex, Jonkman et al. (2002) found a heterozygous 2-bp deletion in the ITGB4 gene (4733delCT). This deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36 and was predicted to delete 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the cytoplasmic domain. Immunoblot analysis showed a beta-4 polypeptide that was 5 kD shorter than normal. Because no full-size protein was detected in vitro and the 450-11A epitope was absent in vivo, the patient was also expected to be heterozygous for a null allele. The authors concluded that deleting the third fibronectin type III repeat, which is thought to interact with BP180/type XVII collagen, is pathogenic.
